guides.title: 10-K risk factors and audited financial statements answer different questions
guides.concept: A Form 10-K contains a business description, risk factors, management commentary and financial statements. A headline profit alone is not a complete picture of business or financial risk.
guides.procedure: Record issuer, annual fiscal period, filing date, business model, material risks, and the audited statement dates before linking a financial metric to a claim.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A classroom issuer reports $40 million revenue and $5 million net income, but its 10-K also describes major customer concentration. The 12.5% margin does not erase disclosed customer risk.
guides.limit: Filing descriptions can be forward-looking or stale, and an auditor opinion does not guarantee future earnings, market price or trading returns.
guides.invalidation: Treat the result as unavailable or inconclusive whenever data vintage, source rights, period alignment, valuation assumptions, undefined denominators or completed observation evidence is missing. Filing descriptions can be forward-looking or stale, and an auditor opinion does not guarantee future earnings, market price or trading returns.
guides.commonError: Treating one favorable earnings figure as proof that the issuer has no meaningful liquidity, customer or regulatory exposure.
guides.selfCheck: Identify the input variables and units used in 10-K risk factors and audited financial statements answer different questions; distinguish the observable result from an unsupported inference and verify a calculation or logical criterion without future information.

guides.title: Gross profit margin and the matching-period cost of sales
guides.concept: Gross margin compares sales after cost of goods sold to total revenue, using comparable accounting periods and units. It does not deduct every operating expense.
guides.procedure: Identify net revenue and associated cost of goods sold for the same reported period, calculate gross profit = revenue − COGS, then divide by revenue.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: $100 million net sales minus $65 million cost of goods sold equals $35 million gross profit; gross margin is 35%, before selling, research and administration.
guides.limit: Different businesses classify production and service costs differently; gross margin is not operating cash flow or total profitability.
guides.invalidation: Treat the result as unavailable or inconclusive whenever data vintage, source rights, period alignment, valuation assumptions, undefined denominators or completed observation evidence is missing. Different businesses classify production and service costs differently; gross margin is not operating cash flow or total profitability.
guides.commonError: Using net income divided by revenue and calling the result gross margin, or mixing quarterly COGS with annual revenue.

guides.title: Current ratio compared with working capital in dollars
guides.concept: The current ratio divides current assets by current liabilities, while net working capital subtracts the liabilities from assets. They use the same balance-sheet date.
guides.procedure: Confirm account classifications and a matching fiscal date; compute ratio only for a positive current-liability denominator and disclose dollar working capital separately.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Current assets of $120 million and current liabilities of $80 million imply current ratio 1.5 and net working capital $40 million.
guides.limit: One positive ratio is not a guarantee of liquidity; receivable quality, inventory turnover, due dates and restricted cash affect realizable funds.
guides.invalidation: Treat the result as unavailable or inconclusive whenever data vintage, source rights, period alignment, valuation assumptions, undefined denominators or completed observation evidence is missing. One positive ratio is not a guarantee of liquidity; receivable quality, inventory turnover, due dates and restricted cash affect realizable funds.
guides.commonError: Presenting a current ratio of 1.5 as $1.50 of cash per dollar of debt without checking asset quality.

guides.title: Enterprise value is not identical to equity market capitalization
guides.concept: A simplified enterprise-value bridge starts with market value of common equity, adds debt and other senior claims when applicable, and subtracts excess cash.
guides.procedure: Define valuation date, share class, price and diluted share count; identify debt and cash conventions before applying an explicit simplified bridge.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Equity market cap $500 million + debt $150 million − excess cash $50 million = simplified enterprise value $600 million, absent other claims.
guides.limit: Preferred interests, minority interests, nonoperating assets, leases and equity dilution may require adjustments; this is not an audited valuation.
guides.invalidation: Treat the result as unavailable or inconclusive whenever data vintage, source rights, period alignment, valuation assumptions, undefined denominators or completed observation evidence is missing. Preferred interests, minority interests, nonoperating assets, leases and equity dilution may require adjustments; this is not an audited valuation.
guides.commonError: Equating market cap with enterprise value while ignoring debt and cash or double-counting cash.

guides.title: WACC weights are capital-structure weights, not equal averaging
guides.concept: Under a simple debt-and-equity model, weighted average cost of capital adds weighted cost of equity to weighted after-tax cost of debt using matching market-value weights.
guides.procedure: Check market value of equity and debt, cost of equity, pretax debt cost and applicable marginal tax rate; confirm weights total one.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Equity share 75% at cost 12%, debt share 25% at pretax cost 6%, tax assumption 20%: WACC = 0.75×12% + 0.25×6%×0.80 = 10.2%.
guides.limit: Real financing includes changing market weights, hybrid claims, tax shields, risk differences and nonconstant rates; this simplified WACC is not a market price forecast.
guides.invalidation: Treat the result as unavailable or inconclusive whenever data vintage, source rights, period alignment, valuation assumptions, undefined denominators or completed observation evidence is missing. Real financing includes changing market weights, hybrid claims, tax shields, risk differences and nonconstant rates; this simplified WACC is not a market price forecast.
guides.commonError: Averaging 12% and 6% to claim 9% WACC without checking financing mix and after-tax borrowing cost.
guides.selfCheck: Identify the input variables and units used in WACC weights are capital-structure weights, not equal averaging; distinguish the observable result from an unsupported inference and verify a calculation or logical criterion without future information.

guides.title: Present value of one hypothetical future cash receipt
guides.concept: A one-period present value divides a promised hypothetical future cash receipt by one plus a consistent periodic discount rate, without confusing it with a bond quote.
guides.procedure: Declare future cash-flow date, cash amount, chosen periodic rate and compounding interval; compute PV=CF/(1+r) and check r is greater than −100%.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: $110 expected one year from now discounted at an illustrative 10% annual rate has a present value of $100, ignoring default and fees.
guides.limit: Forecast cash flows are uncertain, rates may shift, and a simple one-year example is not an independently estimated stock value.
guides.invalidation: Treat the result as unavailable or inconclusive whenever data vintage, source rights, period alignment, valuation assumptions, undefined denominators or completed observation evidence is missing. Forecast cash flows are uncertain, rates may shift, and a simple one-year example is not an independently estimated stock value.
guides.commonError: Applying a monthly rate to an annual cash receipt without reconciling periods, or assuming the chosen rate was empirically verified.

guides.title: Equity DCF and firm DCF must match the proper discount rate
guides.concept: Forecast cash flows belonging to equity holders are discounted using the cost of equity; pre-debt free cash flows to the firm instead use WACC.
guides.procedure: Classify each cash flow before calculating, choose consistent forecast periods and a rate reflecting the appropriate claimholder exposure.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: An analyst models hypothetical next-year FCFF of $100 million but uses the 15% cost of equity instead of the assumed 10% WACC; the model mixes firm cash flows with an equity discount rate.
guides.limit: Even consistently paired cash flows and rates do not validate growth projections or terminal values; an enterprise bridge still needs outstanding claims.
guides.invalidation: Treat the result as unavailable or inconclusive whenever data vintage, source rights, period alignment, valuation assumptions, undefined denominators or completed observation evidence is missing. guides.title: Net income and operating cash flow are distinct accounting views
guides.concept: Accrual earnings can reflect revenue recognized before cash collection, while operating cash flow reflects cash receipts and payments reconciled under accounting standards.
guides.procedure: Read income statements and cash-flow statements from the same reporting period; identify net income and major working-capital movements before comparing.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Net income $12 million with a $9 million increase in receivables, all else held constant, suggests much less cash conversion than the same earnings with immediate collection.
guides.limit: Working-capital movement is not the only cash-flow adjustment; depreciation, payables and deferred taxes also affect the reconciliation.
guides.invalidation: Treat the result as unavailable or inconclusive whenever data vintage, source rights, period alignment, valuation assumptions, undefined denominators or completed observation evidence is missing. Working-capital movement is not the only cash-flow adjustment; depreciation, payables and deferred taxes also affect the reconciliation.
guides.commonError: Calling net income identical to cash generated or assuming all positive cash flow represents distributable free cash.

guides.concept: An annual expense ratio states ongoing operating costs as a fraction of fund assets under a fund's prospectus conventions, distinct from trading spreads and taxes.

guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A $10,000 fictional fund holding with a 0.50% annual expense ratio implies roughly $50 of annualized operating expenses before changing value or tracking effects.
guides.limit: Fees generally accrue through the fund's net asset value and asset values change; the simple $50 figure is illustrative, not a literal annual invoice.

guides.title: Small recurring annual fund costs can compound into material differences
guides.concept: Recurring expense drag changes the amount that remains invested, causing differences in compounded outcomes even when pre-fee market returns are assumed equal.
guides.procedure: Declare initial principal, hypothetical constant annual gross return, annual expense assumption and period; compare two explicitly simplified annual compounding paths.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: On $10,000 with a constant gross 5% yearly assumption, a simplified 1% annual fee drag yields 4% modeled annual net growth versus 5% without fees. Actual fund accrual mechanics differ.
guides.limit: This is a deterministic scenario, not a forecast or exact mutual-fund net-asset-value fee process; taxes, tracking, distributions and volatility are omitted.
guides.invalidation: Treat the result as unavailable or inconclusive whenever data vintage, source rights, period alignment, valuation assumptions, undefined denominators or completed observation evidence is missing. guides.title: Monthly CPI percent change uses comparable index levels
guides.concept: A price-index percent change divides the difference between later and earlier index readings by the earlier compatible reading; index-point change alone is not an inflation rate.
guides.procedure: Confirm the same CPI series, geography, seasonal-adjustment status, base and one-month time interval before computing change as a percent.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: CPI index 300.0 becomes 301.5 next month; month-over-month increase is (301.5/300−1)×100 = 0.50%, not 1.5%.
guides.limit: Rounded index data can change the published one-decimal result, and changing series or seasonal-adjustment convention makes comparisons invalid.
guides.invalidation: Treat the result as unavailable or inconclusive whenever data vintage, source rights, period alignment, valuation assumptions, undefined denominators or completed observation evidence is missing. Rounded index data can change the published one-decimal result, and changing series or seasonal-adjustment convention makes comparisons invalid.

guides.title: Twelve-month CPI change requires the same calendar month one year apart
guides.concept: An over-the-year CPI comparison uses compatible readings exactly twelve months apart; adding twelve rounded monthly inflation reports can differ from the correct ratio.
guides.procedure: Match the same seasonally adjusted or unadjusted series and compare month t with month t−12, using (latest/prior−1)×100.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A CPI index reads 280 in October of one fictional year and 294 in October the next, yielding 5% over the year.
guides.limit: This does not identify the purchasing-power experience of every household; different baskets and data vintages yield different rates.

guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A fictitious GDP growth estimate announced as 2.0% in April is revised to 2.6% in May. An April replay cannot display May's revised number as known evidence.
guides.limit: Seasonal updates, benchmark revisions and source licensing can change data. A latest-only chart is not evidence of historical availability.
guides.invalidation: Treat the result as unavailable or inconclusive whenever data vintage, source rights, period alignment, valuation assumptions, undefined denominators or completed observation evidence is missing. guides.title: Correlation is a standardized linear association, not a causal mechanism
guides.concept: Pearson's sample correlation divides sample covariance by the product of two sample standard deviations for paired observations with nonzero variation.
guides.procedure: Use synchronized pairs and a consistent denominator for covariance and standard deviations; report coefficient in [−1,1] only when both series vary.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Paired series X=[1,2,3], Y=[2,4,6] have Pearson correlation +1; that alone does not prove X causes changes in Y.
guides.limit: Small samples, outliers, nonlinear patterns and shared trends can mislead. Perfect correlation in a three-pair example is not validated economic causation.
guides.invalidation: Treat the result as unavailable or inconclusive whenever data vintage, source rights, period alignment, valuation assumptions, undefined denominators or completed observation evidence is missing. Small samples, outliers, nonlinear patterns and shared trends can mislead. Perfect correlation in a three-pair example is not validated economic causation.
guides.commonError: Claiming two assets with correlation +1 must share the same underlying cause or will remain perfectly correlated.

guides.procedure: Calculate sample dispersion first using n−1, verify n≥2 and define the sampling assumptions; express SEM in the same units as the observations.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Hypothetical observations [1,2,3] have sample standard deviation 1 and standard error 1/√3 ≈0.577, under an IID convention.
guides.limit: Serial dependence, fat tails, selection and nonrepresentative data can invalidate the conventional standard-error interpretation.
guides.invalidation: Treat the result as unavailable or inconclusive whenever data vintage, source rights, period alignment, valuation assumptions, undefined denominators or completed observation evidence is missing. guides.title: Sharpe-style return/risk ratios require consistent measurement intervals
guides.concept: A simple excess-return-to-volatility ratio subtracts a return reference from average return and divides by standard deviation measured over the same frequency.
guides.procedure: Align monthly portfolio returns, monthly risk-free return and monthly dispersion, then state whether any annualization assumes independent stable returns.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Average monthly hypothetical portfolio return 1%, monthly risk-free reference 0.2%, monthly volatility 2% gives unannualized ratio 0.4.
guides.limit: Risk-free rates and returns must share the same horizon; volatility scaling and nonnormal outcomes undermine overconfident inference.
guides.invalidation: Treat the result as unavailable or inconclusive whenever data vintage, source rights, period alignment, valuation assumptions, undefined denominators or completed observation evidence is missing. Risk-free rates and returns must share the same horizon; volatility scaling and nonnormal outcomes undermine overconfident inference.
guides.commonError: Subtracting an annual risk-free yield from a monthly return without conversion and presenting the result as a valid Sharpe ratio.
